To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) centrioles are tightly coupled in PGCs and oogonia; 2) the doublets begin to separate in pre-pubertally arrested GV oocytes and the dissolution is complete by metaphase-I; and, 3) the centrioles are not required for spindle pole formation.

centrioles, present as doublet pairs in primordial germ cells and oogonia, separate and dissolve during oogenesis, and that a single centriole pair remains associated with spindle poles during meiotic maturation.

centrioles in oocytes of mammals are not lost in the germinal vesicle stage as previously thought, but are retained until meiosis resumption and that the centriole doublet breaks apart and is progressively lost as meiosis resumes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the presence and disappearance of centrioles during oogenesis.
the centriole cycle in the mouse oocyte and its role in oocyte meiotic maturation.
the mechanism and time course of the loss of the centrioles from the mammalian oocyte.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
centrioles, present at all stages of oocyte development in the mouse, are progressively reduced during follicular recruitment, meiotic resumption and oocyte maturation.

oocyte maturation is associated with the loss of the two centriole components, Cep135, and GFP-centrin-1, but not with the loss of Cep164 and Cep152, which are maintained in the PCM of mature oocytes.
the centrioles of the mouse oocyte are lost by dissolution, rather than by degradation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the centriole doublet is a stable feature of the mouse oocyte until the resumption of meiosis, at which time it undergoes a partial reduction in number and a progressive disassociation from the PCM, which is complete at the metaphase of meiosis I. This
the mouse oocyte is born with two functional centrioles and that these doublets are lost in a stepwise manner, with the first sign of dissolution occurring at follicular recruitment.
the mouse oocyte is born with a doublet of centrioles that is maintained until the onset of meiotic maturation and then undergoes a partial reduction that is uncoupled to microtubule activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
centriole loss is not complete at the onset of meiosis, but rather is a dynamic process that is initiated during follicular recruitment of the GV oocytes and is accelerated during oocyte maturation.
centrioles are lost during oogenesis, and that this loss is not a result of microtubule disassembly, but rather of an active, centriole-dependent process.

centriole reduction in oocytes does not follow a single pathway but rather occurs in stages, beginning with the loss of centriole association in the PCM, followed by the separation of centrioles and finally by the loss of the remaining single centriole from the PCM.
